why: It is a household-by-household count of the outbuildings of three hamlets, by function, which is the strongest kind of evidence the record has for what stood on a farmstead and is what populates our farmyards. Its limits are that the survey was made in July 1972, a quarter century after the postwar land reform and well into mechanization, when, on this project's reading and not the paper's, the draft ox and horse had largely left Tohoku farms, so the barn and livestock-shed frequencies are a floor rather than a premodern figure and some sheds are twentieth-century equipment; that it is the cold, snowy northeast and not the whole country; that it is three hamlets of one town, 87 households, a sample the author calls surprisingly rich in outbuildings for Tohoku (4.38 a household, against 3.90 and 2.97 in the two surveys the paper compares it with); that the figures the record takes are mostly the row for the 38 farms whose main house was built in or before 1944, which is an older house and not a premodern one; that its table gives average counts per household by use, with a building of several uses counted once under each, so the figures cannot be added up into a number of buildings, and the record reads each one as an upper bound on the share of households owning one - the two agree only where no household kept two; and that the paper's own note 3 says that splitting farm uses out into separate outbuildings happened mainly between the Meiji era and the postwar years, here perhaps because stables were built inside the house as horse breeding grew, pushing other uses out. Where the record has a count from before 1868 (a village record of 1824, a village count of 1885 read back to the bakumatsu), the map is calibrated to that instead, and those counts find far fewer outbuildings.
It dates the end of the walled ward, which is why the Chinese half of our block-gate argument turns on palings across streets rather than ward walls.

It gives the Ming inner city's wall perimeter, the size of the city the Beijing drum tower served. Wikipedia itself marks it as needing citations and as partly translated from Chinese; its 24-kilometre perimeter carries no citation of its own. It gives the inner city as a perimeter, not as side lengths, and its one statement of shape (a roughly square city with "the east and west walls slightly longer") is wrong, since the plan is wider east-west than north-south, so only the perimeter is taken from this page and any east-west and north-south figures are read off a map. Beijing was the imperial capital and the largest walled city of its era, so its inner city is an upper bound on what one drum tower timed, not the size of a provincial town.

It is a measured count of what grew in surviving homestead groves, including the fruit trees among them. The persimmon is among the three most frequent species in only one of the four districts, the Tonami scattered-farmstead groves. Elsewhere cedar, chestnut, pine or evergreen broadleaves lead. So it supports a persimmon in a grove of the Tonami kind, not in every homestead grove. Its species counts and its note that cedar dominated every grove of the three summer-green regions, planted in rows at Iide and Tonami and clipped like a hedge at Hikawa, are what show the planted windbreak as led by one tree yet mixed. It is a short abstract of a few homesteads per region (five at Tonami), and gives no areas or tree counts.

It divides the commons into the two kinds a map draws differently - forest taken for fuel, timber and leaf litter, and open grass and riverbank land cut for fodder and thatch. Its one citation, a 1973 paper on place-names, backs only the names such as 内山 and 内野, so the division into two kinds that we use rests on the article alone. It gives no sizes or locations, and says nothing of Chinese village commons.

It says that the rivers pass on one side of the village while a dug channel about a meter wide runs through it to every household - the same pairing the record already shows at Harie, now in a Chinese village. It cites nothing for its water passages (its only references are a Michelin travel-guide page and a county conservation plan whose link is dead). It dates the bringing of water into the village to the Ming Yongle reign (1403-1424), when a geomancer re-planned the layout, but it does not date the channel itself. Hongcun is a wealthy lineage village, planned by a geomancer and rebuilt with salt-merchant money, and what stands today is a restored tourist site. It is not a small farming hamlet, and its channel carries household water, not irrigation.

It describes a famous East Asian fortress form built round, which this page uses to show that even there the square was as common, so that a curved wall is not the East Asian answer to the corner. It is used with the Chinese article beside it, which states which form is the more widespread; and a tulou is a rural clan dwelling, one building, recruited here into an argument about castle baileys and city walls of a far larger order.

It says that a castle town, not only a post station, kept a relay, and where in the town it stood. It is a short article resting on one encyclopedia entry, and it gives no size for the quarter or its stables.

It is the compact scholarly statement of what a Japanese road town looked like and how large it was, written by a historian, an architectural historian and a historical geographer, which is what a town map strung along a road needs. It is strongest for the five great highways; it gives ranges and typical forms, not any one town's measured plan. Its size (300 to 600 houses, 30 to 60 inns) is the Tokaido's, the busiest road, and its inn counts are from an 1843 survey; it says stations off the great highways were smaller, so for a town on a lesser road the figure is an upper bound. The busy road's look, two-story plank-roofed inns filling the frontage, is a late-Edo form.

It states in words that the post, market and temple-gate towns of the Edo period almost all took the street-town form, which is the frequency behind this record's plan knob, and names the one-sided variant. That "almost all" is one encyclopedia's generalization, not a count, and it covers only those three kinds of town, not castle towns or small towns in general.

It gives the size of a county seat's wall as a class, which is what a walled town's rampart is scaled against. It is an encyclopedia article that cites no source for either its grading or its 4 to 10 m height. Its grades are rough and its own class assignments overlap: class 3 is "each provincial capital", but class 2 already lists several provincial capitals. It qualifies that the smallest walls were found especially on the western frontier and that many eastern county seats were larger than western prefectural cities. So a class gives a range for a county seat's wall, not a length fixed by the town's rank. It says nothing about a Japanese town, which in the Edo period was mostly unwalled.

It says these were commercial crops of the field, grown for sale and for processing, restricted by the shogunate's rules on what a field might grow and later encouraged as local specialties, often under a domain's monopoly - which is why a mulberry or a tea planting is drawn as a crop rather than a dooryard tree. That is our reading: the entries do not say where on a holding these crops stood, and do not rule out a few bushes by a house or along a field's edge. The two entries differ in emphasis - one says the domains encouraged the crops, the other that the shogunate restricted them - and neither says how much of any village's ground they took. Both are short entries (the Nipponica entry rests on Yoshinaga Akira's 1973 study of domain monopolies), and they cover Edo-period Japan only; applying them to a place modeled on China is by analogy.

It places the custom at the village's entrance roads and crossroads and lists its physical forms, among them a rope stretched across the road and one fixed to a boundary tree. It is drawn from customs still practiced today: one 2013 book on the rope form, a weather-association column, municipal education-board pages and a Chiba prefectural museum's pages. Its list of forms rests on one of those Chiba museum pages. It dates the custom only as "from of old", and dates none of its forms to the Edo period or earlier. It gives no share of villages that practiced any one form.

It defines an academy as a privately founded school, sometimes under official direction, set apart from the official schools, with its own school lands, a head called the shanzhang, and three functions: lecturing, offerings at its shrine, and examining students. It is thinly footnoted (most of its history cites one popular book on the academies of Changhua), with no sizes, plans or counts of academies per city. What an academy was changed by era: private lecture halls under the Song and Yuan, suppressed more than once under the Ming, and under state supervision after the Qing ordered academies in every province in 1733. A claim taken from it should name the dynasty it holds for.

It defines the hall at a temple's center that houses the principal image, and it says that hall goes by other names depending on era and sect: kondo at temples founded from the Asuka to the early Heian period, chudo in Tendai, butsuden in Zen, daiyu hoden in Obaku. Some temples have both a kondo and a hondo, and the article says no clear line can be drawn between the names. It is a Wikipedia stub whose two listed references are not tied to any statement, so it carries the definition and not a detail. It covers Japan only and says nothing of Chinese temples, which our setting is equally modeled on. It gives no sizes.

It shows that a town's time bell could hang at a temple: three of the thirteen bells it names are at temples (Tenryū-ji in Shinjuku, Sensō-ji in Asakusa, Nion-ji in Kaizu). One more is at a shrine, and the rest are at a castle, a town street or a present-day park. It is a page with no sources, it says it is incomplete, and it gives no dates, no count of how many towns kept a bell, and nothing on who rang it. So it supports "sometimes at a temple", not "often". The ja.wikipedia article 石町時の鐘, which cites a 1979 history of Chūō Ward, lists Edo's nine authorized bells, most of them at temples.

It states that founding houses, historical or legendary, held the village offices such as headman generation after generation and held first place at the places of worship and in the shared land and water - the link between the headman and the village's oldest house. Its limits: a short stub article resting on two encyclopedia entries it names in its bibliography, with no footnotes to individual statements, no period narrower than "before modern times" and no region narrower than Japan, and nothing on where a founding house stood in the village. It also hedges its own claim: where a founding house did not hold the office, it still had a say as the main house of the village's branch families, so the office was usual rather than certain. A closer signed source is readable on Kotobank: Fukuda Ajio's entry in the Heibonsha world encyclopedia (改訂新版 世界大百科事典) places the pattern in the early modern period and says the founding houses often, not always, held the village offices by hereditary monopoly.

It says that naming a place from its terrain is a common way of naming, most of all for small-scale terrain and old names, and that many names' origins are disputed or unknown - the ground and the limit of reading a village's name for where it stands. Its limits: it is a general encyclopedia article that gives no count of how many names are topographic. Its terrain passage rests on a single citation to Sugimura's 1978 book on place names, for which the article itself asks a page number. Its sentence that many origins are disputed or unknown cites nothing, and the article carries maintenance tags asking for citations. Its terrain examples are old generic Japanese terms, not modern ones, and it also treats Chinese and Korean naming, but only in passages we do not cite. A closer public source exists that we have not read: Yanagita Kunio's study of Japanese small place names, 地名の研究 (1936), on Aozora Bunko.

It gives the one statement read on how common the form is by region - few nationally, few in Kansai, said to be many in Kanto - and that no new one has in principle been allowed since 1948. The ones that survive are only those licensed under the Meiji-era burial rules that came before, and unlicensed ones do not count as legal graveyards. So where they survive has passed through two modern laws, and is not a map of where the form was once made. It reports the regional pattern only as hearsay, and it says nothing of premodern frequency.

It gives the number of temples in one planned temple quarter of an early Edo castle town: 33 Soto temples, Chōshō-ji among them, standing along the tree-lined avenue that leads to Chōshō-ji, which the second Tsugaru lord moved to Hirosaki in 1610 as the castle was built. It lists the temples but does not map them, so it does not show whether all 33 face that one avenue or some stand on streets off it. The article itself calls so many temples of one sect in one place rare nationwide, so this is an upper bound set by a domain's deliberate policy, not a typical temple quarter. It is a short article resting on city and tourist-guide pages, and it gives no sizes.

It says the house served as Shitennoji's retained temple carpenters up to the early modern period and lost the temple's stipend in 1868, when the temple lost its lands - a craft household kept on a stipend by one temple. It carries a banner saying it lacks sources, and its chronology - the stipend and its loss in 1868 included - cites nothing; the firm's early history is its own tradition as the article relays it. It describes one house at Shitennoji, one of Japan's oldest and greatest temples, in a major city, so it shows the arrangement at a great temple and not that an ordinary town or village temple kept carpenters; it gives neither the stipend's size nor how many carpenters there were, and says nothing of where the carpenters lived.

It gives the share of rice in the everyday grain by kind of district - even paddy districts mixing in large amounts, dry-field districts eating millet and barley with a little rice, the Kanto dry-field belt eating rice that was 70 to 80 percent barley, and one paddy district cooking about two parts rice to half a part barley - which brackets how much of a farmer's grain was not rice. Its figures trace to a folklore dictionary of food (2013) and the prefectural oral-history volumes (1988-90), which record the diets of about 1930 as recalled in the 1980s, so they describe farming after the Meiji-era changes and are not an Edo-period count; the article says only that most could not eat plain rice as a staple until at least 1955-64, and it carries a notice that it needs sources; it gives the mix in the pot, not a share of the whole diet.

It is a named example of a farm drain (an akusui channel) serving an Edo-period irrigation system and carrying the fields' spent water to a river. The article does not say when the drain was dug, and the route it gives is today's channel: a city-managed minor river joined by a modern trunk drain, with a pumping station planned. It is one channel on the Kanto lowland; it says nothing of how a single field's drain reached it, nor of drains in hill valleys.

It is the one page found that gives storehouses as a ratio to households, the figure a town-wide count needs. It reports the figure as hearsay, the count is a modern one, of a stock that grew after the town's great fire of 1880 (the page itself gives that fire as one reason for the storehouses, and shows brick ones among them), so it describes a Meiji-to-Showa town more than an Edo one, and Kitakata is famous precisely for having unusually many; another page counts about 4,000.

It is one of the few public pages that measures a county wall in section and its moat on each side, and says every gate had a barbican and a drawbridge. It is one coastal town that was also a garrison seat, so its wall and gates may be heavier than an inland county's; its metric figures are the article's own conversions of the gazetteer's zhang and chi. Its moat is uneven - about 16 m wide on the east, 14 m on the south, 42 m on the west - and joins rivers on the west and east, so the widest figure is not a typical moat. It has no moat on the north because that wall stood on the seawall itself, a form few towns shared.

It gives one measured masugata court and records the gate's early name as an earthen causeway. Its 27 by 38 m carries no footnote on the page; the footnoted figure is the court's 320 tsubo (about 1,060 square metres), which agrees with it. The page calls this court unusually large, built so to guard the western enclosure (Nishinomaru), and the widest of Edo castle's surviving masugata, so its size is a ceiling, not a typical gate.

It is the one page read that shows a small Japanese town's entry posts on the ground. It names its source, the Kitsuki city history (杵築市誌), without page numbers, and Kitsuki was a castle town, the seat of a small domain, so its posts may be more than an ordinary market town kept; it gives no building sizes.

It places the market god's shrine or stone at a village boundary, a landing, a bridge foot or a crossroads, and says a market is inferred from where one stands; one entry (Kitami's) dates the market-god festival to the year's first market, while the others give about the tenth of the first month, the year's start and end, or the storehouse opening or Little New Year, and one says few places fix a day. One entry says most surviving stones now stand in village shrine precincts, so a stone's present place is not always its first; and it gives no size for the shrine or the stone.

It shows that a masugata gate stood on the outer works of the shogun's own castle, not only at its core. It is a short article with no references at all (the page carries Wikipedia's banner for an unsourced article). It gives the 36 mitsuke as a traditional figure ("there are said to have been 36"), not a count of gates, so the number sets the scale and is not an exact tally. It is about Edo, the largest castle in Japan, so it says nothing about the gates of a provincial castle town.

It is a real Edo-period canal cut through a city to bring freight to the townspeople's doors, the case a river city's in-city canal is. It is one canal, and a small one - a shallow barge cut, not a harbor channel - so its width is the narrow end of the range. The article gives the width and depth (8 m, usually about 30 cm) in the present tense without saying whether they are the 1614 cut or the channel as it runs today, after boats stopped in 1920 and the channel was changed in the 1930s. It names and places its nine boat-entry basins but gives no size for any of them. The article cites newspaper pieces, city materials and one dictionary entry.

It gives the plot sizes that show a magistracy's staff lived outside its compound on ground of their own, one of the two forms of our Imperial Magistrate's staff housing. It is a personal page quoting modern reference works without page numbers. It describes one city only - Edo, the shogun's capital, from about 1660 (when Hatchobori became the magistracies' group housing) to the 1860s - and the staff of that city's two town magistracies, about 25 officers and 100 to 120 constables each; it bears on a capital's magistracy, not a county seat's. The page places both officers and constables at Hatchobori, though the 200 to 300 tsubo sentence does not itself name the place. A constable's plot of about 100 tsubo was mostly let to tenants (scholars, physicians, artists), the constable living in a house of about 30 tsubo, so the plot is not one household's yard.

It is the one page read that gives a count of gates below the great cities - one to several blocks, against one to each block in a large town - and it describes the gate's form. Dictionary and encyclopedia entries that give no references of their own. The entries place the gates chiefly in the great cities - Edo, Kyoto, Osaka - and the form, the closing hour and the keeper's night round they give are the city of Edo's. The count is one sentence of the old Sekai Daihyakka's entry on the gate, written of the great cities and not of any named town. Its 町 can be read as a ward-block rather than a town (a large block with a gate of its own, small blocks sharing one), so it gives a shape for a small town, not a figure. The Nipponica entry is by Inagaki Fumio, a period-drama consultant and novelist rather than a historian, and the entries give the great gate's width in two slightly different figures.

It is the one page read that says a castle town always kept riding grounds, gives their usual shape in ken, and places several real ones against a moat, a senior retainer's house or a street. The encyclopedia entry (signed by Tamai Tetsuo, a historian of Edo's buildings and city) summarizes, and its size of about 100 ken by 10 ken is a typical figure hedged as the common case, with every example drawn from Edo, the shogun's capital, so a lesser castle town's ground may differ from it (Ako's was 5 ken wide on two and a half cho of riverbank). The gazetteer entries are excerpts, each describing one Japanese castle town of the Edo period or just before it.

It puts a domain's gunpowder store inside the castle, in its second bailey, which is where the record keeps the armory. It cites nothing for this passage, so it carries the idea (a stone-built powder store, 煙硝蔵, in the western part of an Edo-period domain castle's second bailey) and not a rule. It hedges the store's place as apparent, it does not date the store, and it is one castle. The same article puts the arms magistrate's office (武具奉行役所) in the third bailey, not beside the powder store, so on its own it does not support an armory in the second bailey.

It says where the tea stalls stood - the roadside, the temple and shrine precincts and gates, the crowded amusement quarters - and that most were stalls whose keepers lived elsewhere, some open only in blossom season, which is why a tea stall is placed by where the crowd is and may be drawn as a light stall. Their examples are all from Japan's great cities in the mid-to-late Edo period: Edo's Ryogoku, Asakusa and Ueno from about 1740-1770, and Kyoto's Gion and Shijo riverbed. They show where tea stalls stood in a metropolis, not how many a town or village had.

It places the Chinese village granary in the village, which is the Chinese half of the setting's ancestry. Its limits are that it is a short article whose own references are two modern Chinese historical dictionaries (1990, 2000) and one line of the Sui history; that it spans many dynasties in a few lines; that by its own account the village siting was often an aim rather than the practice (the Tang granaries stood mostly in prefecture and county seats, and Zhu Xi's were run by rich households who abused them); and that it says nothing of the building.

It gives a small domain's castle at both ends - stone walls stacked in four tiers to 60 m in all, the third-bailey wall alone 22 m (found on repair to reach 31 m), and a keep only 15 m high. Its walls are famous because they are exceptional, and the 60 m is four walls climbing a 66 m hill, not one wall - the article itself gives Osaka's 33 m as the tallest single wall. Its keep is the smallest of the twelve that survive, not of all that were built: a three-storey turret of 1660, altered in 1877, which some scholars count as a turret rather than a keep, because no new keeps were built after 1615. So it is a floor only among survivors. It is a Japanese stone castle of 1597-1673. The 60 m rests on a Shogakukan castle guide, the 31 m on the castle office's newsletter, and the 15 m has no citation of its own.

Its comparison of the three great quarters - inside the town with a fence on one side, at the edge with an earthen wall, cut off by a wall and fields - gives the three forms a walled quarter could take, and it places Osaka's on new ground at the town's west. It is one the article itself has flagged since February 2012 as short of sources: its comparison of the three quarters carries no footnote and rests only on the two place-name dictionaries it lists (Heibonsha's and Kadokawa's), so it gives the three forms and not a checked fact about any one quarter's gates or walls (a Kansai University study of Shinmachi's layout, 2002, which the article cites, is the closer source for the quarter itself); it gives the quarter's blocks and its courtesans but not its area, and the three quarters it compares are those of the three greatest cities.

It describes the fish ponds as a reporter sees them today, from the air ("a vast blue-and-green chessboard") and on foot. Its history is heritage promotion. Its one source from the period is an opening couplet by the Tang poet Lu Guimeng (ditches and banks, silkworm trays and fish traps round Lake Tai). The couplet shows mulberry and fish farmed together but says nothing of how the ponds were laid out, and the article cites nothing else for its history. It claims the system began in the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, over 2,500 years ago. It says only that the low ground was drained by a water works of "lengthwise channels and crosswise embankments" (纵浦横塘), with the ponds dug out and their mud heaped up as dikes. It gives no layout of the ponds themselves before the present day. The landscape it shows is also a managed one: it says many ponds were abandoned or shrank before 2013, and that the system has since been protected by regulation and developed for tourism.

It states that irrigation water was held and allocated by village associations under customary practice and that the order of intake was itself fought over in the courts, which is why this page will not give a kawata quarter a headwater tap. The article is a stub marked for expansion.

It is the one page found that describes a floating log boom in Japan: a main rope run from the far bank at a sharp angle to the stream, floats tied along it, drawing the logs to the near bank. Every source it gives is modern (a paper company's forestry history of 1976, a Hokkaido town history of 1993, a forestry encyclopedia of 1984), its one example is the former imperial Kiso forest (a Meiji-and-later estate), whose main rope was four 20 cm ropes of sarunashi vine and two 6 cm steel cables, and its one dated picture, of a landing boom in Hokkaido, is of 1948. It says timber was floated by river until the late 1940s and early 1950s, and calls the boom a timber-floating device "originally" (元来), but gives no date for when it began; its silence is not evidence that the boom is modern. It is good for the boom's shape and its names (the landing boom, the holding boom) as modern Japan practiced them; that the boom is older must be shown from elsewhere. The catch rope of a tsunaba, stretched across the Kiso to stop floated timber, is on record from 1422 (see tsunaba-nikkoku and nishikori-tsunaba), but no premodern record was found of floats strung along such a rope.

It dates an Edo-period river intake and gives two reasons its site was chosen: the ground there is high enough to carry the water by gravity onto the plateau and on to Edo, and the river is thrown against a ridge on its south bank so that the water gathers toward the other bank. It names the two together and does not say which counted for more, so it supports the bank where the water gathers as one reason for an intake's site, not the only one. The reason for the site is hedged ("thought to be"), it describes the weir in the present tense and does not say that the weir or the intake is unchanged since the Edo period, and it is one intake of one aqueduct, which gives no angle at which the intake leaves the river.

Its statement that each county was limited to one monastery with a maximum of two monks is the one readable figure for the size of an ordinary Ming temple, and it points to a very small median; it is one edict, for which the page gives no year, placing it only under its heading for the 1370s, and describes as a one-moment suppression order with nothing on its enforcement or duration, so reading it as the dynasty's ordinary or median temple is this record's own inference; and it says nothing of the great urban monasteries.

It attests that broadleaf coppice was cut back, leaving the roots, every 10 to 20 years for firewood and charcoal (a figure the article itself does not cite), and separately that leaf litter and undergrowth were carried off every year as fertilizer and fodder, which is the worked floor this page draws; no stand densities. For the fields its limits are two: that dry fields lie on the slopes with the satoyama rests on one region's folk classification (the Yoshino mountains of Nara, where the fields count as part of the satoyama), and that most satoyama had become red pine, grass or bare hill by the early modern period is one author's reading (Arioka 2004) of Edo-period gazetteer pictures, which the same article qualifies with sustainable use after the shogunate's forest-protection policy of 1666.

It is our worked example of a waterfront settlement making new ground out of the earth dug for its own castle, which is the kind of thing that explains why a town's blocks near the water are newer and more regular than the ones behind them. It is one episode in one city, its dates are the traditional ones, and Edo's scale is far beyond anything we draw - so what carries across is the sequence, not the acreage.

We use it for a Chinese county seat's moat as a worked waterway: tied to its river for navigation, fresh water and drainage, and dredged when a magistrate had it done. It is one Yangtze-delta town whose moat was tidal rather than fed from upstream, so it speaks to a moat kept full by its river and to dredging as an official's act, not to the upstream-intake and downstream-return arrangement these maps draw; the 1753 dredging is a single dated event with no interval or cycle behind it, so it attests that dredging happened rather than a maintenance rhythm; and the article gives its moat two different lengths (1,620 zhang in its lead, some 1,500 in its moat section), so its own measurements are not consistent.

It is the other half of the naming question: it tells us what a dobashi actually is, which is what lets our record say that the plank bridge and the earthen bridge are two different objects rather than two words for one. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary with no measurements and no dating of the technique.

We use it for one physical fact that decides how a navigation cut is drawn and labeled on our maps: a canal needs to be level, small irregularities in the ground being taken up by cuttings and embankments, and where a canal meets a river or the sea at a different level the device that connects the two is a gated chamber, the pound lock - whose double-gated form the article dates to tenth-century China, which puts it in period for this setting rather than making it an anachronism. Its center of gravity is the British canal age. Two things it is asked for go beyond plain physics and should be treated as unchecked: the tenth-century date is a historical claim resting on the article alone, and "a canal must be level" is true of a NAVIGATION cut and false of an irrigation canal, which runs at a designed fall - nothing here transfers to the comb net. <!-- The period example a later pass should chase instead is the Minuma Tsusenbori, the lock-gate canal already registered here from the rural-engineering society's page. -->

It states the parish logic our burial grounds rest on, in three parts: temple membership was not an individual affair but the household's, the household's main benefit was the funerary and continuing memorial services the temple provided for all its members, and the affiliation was certified by the local temple and the village officials. That is why a graveyard on these maps is the hall's own yard rather than a plot held apart from it. Its limits are that it describes a state-mandated anti-Christian registration specific to Tokugawa Japan while this setting reaches the same arrangement by another route, so the mechanism differs even where the outcome matches.

It describes the one practice found that trains against a post, in the words a reader can check. Its limits are that it is flagged by Wikipedia itself since 2021 for thin sourcing, whose one footnote for this practice is a modern popular book (Tsumoto Yō's 勝者の極意); that it describes the practice as the school teaches it today and does not itself date the standing timber to the Edo period; that it describes one regional family of schools (Jigen-ryū and offshoots such as Yakumaru Jigen-ryū), barred from being taught outside the Satsuma domain, not the practice of samurai at large; and that it gives the post no size, count or setting.

It gives the order of the three parts of the shogun's palace, and where the family's quarters stood against the lord's own rooms, which is the room order our residence plans take. Its limits are that it describes the shogun's palace, the largest in the country and not a provincial posting: the three-part division, the Ooku walled off and reached by the one Osuzu corridor, and the rule that no man but the shogun entered it are the shogun's arrangements, while the page's only word on lesser houses (the older Heibonsha Ooku entry quoted beneath) says daimyo and hatamoto houses divided a front, the omote, from a back, the oku - two parts, not three. Both entries are by historians and the Nipponica entry names its sources (the Tokyo Shishiko and Naito Akira's Edo to Edo-jo).

It is the one readable record found of dogs housed inside an official's compound, and it gives the shelters' buildings and sizes from the account books. The shelters were for sick and ownerless dogs under the shogunate's policy of the time, not hunting kennels, and the Nakano buildings were on a pound's scale, so neither their form nor their size stands for a household's kennel. Its figures are the account books' figures at second hand, through the historians it cites, and were not read from the books themselves.
